newsitem.title: JORDAN: U.S. strike leaves Saddam unshaken, diplomats say.
newsitem.headline: U.S. strike leaves Saddam unshaken, diplomats say.

text.p: Punitive U.S. missile strikes against Iraq on Tuesday exposed Baghdad's vulnerability to Western military might but are unlikely to shake President Saddam Hussein's grip on power, diplomats said.
They said the attack on Iraqi air defence targets, one of the biggest military strike on Iraq since the 1991 Gulf war, was more likely to turn public anger on Washington than Saddam.
"They might inflict technical and material damage, but psychologically the U.S. has once again given the (Iraqi) people a united enemy," one diplomat said.

Baghdad said five people were killed in the attack, which U.S. President Bill Clinton described as a response to Iraqi troops entering the Kurdish city of Arbil. It said the missiles hit civilian areas as well as military sites.
Saddam defiantly called on his pilots to hit back at planes overflying Iraq and declared Western-imposed "no-fly" zones in northern and southern Iraq "null and void".
"The United States attack may just have increased their siege mentality," said another diplomat. "Once again they feel alone against the rest of the world."

But he said despite the sense of isolation, Saddam had shown up divisions among countries that had united against him after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. Russia and China criticised the missile attacks and France notably declined to voice its support.
"However weak his own position, he always shows up the splits in his opponents," he said.
Outside the oil-rich Gulf states, still haunted by memories of Kuwait's invasion, the Arab world criticised Washington and stood up strongly for Iraq's right to defend its territorial unity.
Iraqi opposition figures in Jordan said the strikes had been ineffective.

A former government official said the U.S. attack came too late to stop Saddam from taking Arbil, together with fighters from the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP). Baghdad says its forces will complete their withdrawal on Tuesday.
"If the KDP can keep control there he can happily withdraw," he said. "He's already achieved his aim".

Other Iraqi opposition figures in Amman said whatever the United States threw at Iraq, Saddam was unlikely to lose his instinct for survival, which saw him through eight years of war with Iran in the 1980s and comprehensive defeat in the 1991 Gulf War.
"In the end he will do anything to cling on to power," said Iraqi defector Haroun Mohammad. "He will make concessions if he has to."

But diplomats said Saddam's fiery response to Tuesday's strike could escalate the confrontation, piling further losses on his country which is already suffering from six years of crippling trade sanctions imposed after it invaded Kuwait.
"If he takes them on directly he must know he's going to get in trouble," one diplomat said.

He said Iraq had already blown its chance to start exporting $2 billion worth of oil under a U.N. "oil-for-food" deal, and a regular U.N. review on Tuesday of sanctions against Baghdad could hardly recommend lifting the six-year-old embargo when Saddam was in such open confrontation with Washington.
